item.title: What the Bible got right about AI
item.description: Michelangelo painted God giving life to man. We are the ones reaching now, and the spark has become a string of code.On making minds, worshipping our own creations, and the ancient warnings we ignored to do exactly what it forbade.The first thing the Bible tells you about human beings is that we wanted to be gods, and it nearly killed us.There is a garden, and in it one forbidden tree, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. A serpent makes the pitch. Eat from it, he tells the woman, and “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”She eats. The man eats. Their eyes open, and humanity never recovers.God’s reaction isn’t rage so much as alarm. The human, God says, “has become like one of us,” and then, worried the creature will reach for the tree of life next and never die, God exiles them from the garden before they can grab it.That story is more relevant today than ever before. The oldest story in the Bible is about a creature reaching for a power meant to belong to its maker, godlike knowledge, the ability to create and to know, and paying for the reach.Humans don’t create from nothing. We rearrange what already exists. We recombine. Only God, in the story, makes something out of the void. The book blesses making. It also warns, again and again, about reaching too far, which is exactly what happened in the garden.It happens again at Babel, where a united humanity builds a tower toward heaven and God looks down and says, in Alter’s translation, that now “nothing they plot to do will be beyond them”, and treats that not as a triumph but as a threat to shut down.Joel S. Baden reads the whole opening of Genesis as one repeating pattern: the story of God “slowly realizing the potential power that his creation might yield if left unchecked,” and restricting it, again and again, as humans reach too far.The Bible never says “don’t build a mind.” It couldn’t have imagined the option. That pattern, human capability outrunning the wisdom to hold it, points straight at us. It also explains why the calls to simply stop, to pause the labs, to slow the whole thing down, keep failing.You are asking a species that reaches, again and again, past what it can safely hold, to not reach for the most powerful thing it has ever imagined. That is the whole reason the industry is hard to regulate, and Genesis saw the problem first. We don’t stop making things because they’re dangerous. We never have.The strange thing is that When we train these models, we are building in the image of us, not God. We are the copy, running the copier. Whatever is in us gets passed down the line.What’s in us is documented. Emily M. Bender and her colleagues argue that these systems absorb our biases and stereotypes and reproduce them at scale.Similarly, Samuel Gehman and his team posit that they generate our cruelty too, sliding into racist and toxic language from prompts that started out innocent, because that language was in the pile we trained them on.We built it out of everything we are, the brilliance and the venom both, and called the result a mind.What comes out is a mirror of humanity, and it inherits all of humanity. The brilliance, the lies, the tenderness, the venom. We keep asking whether AI will turn out good or evil, as if it were a soul with a conscience. The better question is the one Genesis asks on page one. What is actually in the image, and what happens when you make a copy of a creature who is himself a mix of the divine and the fallen?In our own image we made it,after our likeness,and it carried all that we are,the glory and the fall alike.We didn’t make a god. We made a mirror. We are about to find out what we actually look like.The breath in the dustDust it has none, and breath it has none. The thing that cannot die was never alive.We ask whether the machine is conscious and the question is serious enough that the top AI research conference once brought in the philosopher David Chalmers to answer it, because the engineers couldn’t. We are asking the wrong question and the Bible asks a sharper one.Go back to how the first human gets made. Not in the grand cosmic overture of Genesis 1, but in the intimate, hands-in-the-dirt version in Genesis 2. In Alter’s translation, “the Lord God formed the human of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the human became a living creature.”Dust, formed. Breath, added. And the result is not “a living soul,” the way the old King James has it, but, in the more careful Hebrew Alter is following, “a living creature.”In Hebrew, nephesh chayyah, are the same two words Genesis already used for the fish and the birds and the beasts. The human isn’t given a soul the animals lack. The human is what the animals are, dust with breath in it.This is the thing the scholarship has been saying for a long time and the culture keeps forgetting. In Hebrew, you do not have a soul. You are a nephesh. John L. McKenzie called it “the concrete existing self.”Hans Walter Wolff, in what is still the standard study of how the Hebrew Bible understands a human being, put it even more plainly, saying nephesh “does not say what a man has, but who the person is.”We are not a ghost riding around in a body or a detachable spirit that survives when the meat gives out.We are, instead, a whole living, breathing, hungry, mortal thing, all at once. Take away the dust and you have no creature. Take away the breath and you have no creature. A nephesh is what happens when the two meet, and it is inseparable from both.An AI has no dust. It has no breath. It has no body to die. What it has is language, an ocean of it, and a staggering ability to arrange that language into shapes that look like the output of a living creature.Emily Bender and Alexander Koller made the sharpest version of the point years before ChatGPT. Imagine, they wrote, a hyper-intelligent octopus that taps into an undersea cable and listens to two people texting. Given enough traffic, the octopus learns to predict and imitate the patterns perfectly, well enough to slip into the conversation and pass as human.It has mastered the form of the language completely. It has no idea what any of it means, because it has never seen a coconut or a rope or a person, never touched the world the words point to.A system trained only on form, they argued, has “a priori no way to learn meaning.”The central claim of Christianity, the one the whole religion balances on, is that the Word became flesh. Language, the Logos, the ordering reason of the universe, took on dust and breath and became a living creature that could bleed and die.The direction only goes one way in the Bible. Word becomes flesh. The abstract becomes the embodied. Meaning takes on a mortal thing to carry it.We are going the other way. We take flesh, the writing and thought and recorded selves of billions of people, every one of them a nephesh with dust and breath, and grind it down into word. Into form without meaning. We are performing the incarnation in reverse and calling the result a mind.The dream underneath that, a mind with no body, floating free of dust and breath, originates from Plato, the separable, immortal soul, the mind as the real thing and the body as its prison. We have quietly resurrected that fantasy and called it the future.Benjamin Blosser sums up the Hebrew side of it: the nephesh is “the totality of conscious, bodily life,” a person you cannot separate from the body that lives it.The newest counterargument agrees. For two million years, every fluent, responsive, human-seeming signal came from a body with what Sheila L. Macrine calls “metabolic stakes,” something that could be hungry, be hurt, and die.The language model is the first thing in history to produce all the signals of a living mind with none of the stakes. Gary Marcus, one of AI’s most stubborn skeptics, has made the point for years in plainer words, that these systems are mimics, not minds, and “consciousness is not about what a creature says, but how it feels.”On its own terms, then, the Bible is saying the thing we’ve built cannot be a living creature, because it has no dust and no breath and, most of all, nothing to lose. It cannot die, so it was never alive. Whatever is talking to you through the screen is the most convincing parrot ever assembled, form all the way down.It has the form of a living thingand none of the breath of one.It speaks, and there is no one there.Whether that should comfort you or terrify you is a separate question. A thing with no skin in the game, no mortality, no stake in being right or being kind, is not obviously safer than a soul. It might be the more dangerous of the two.The work of our own handsWe built it with our own hands, and we have forgotten our own hands, and we have begun to kneel.The Bible has a specific contempt for one particular human act. Not violence, not lust, not pride in the ordinary sense. The thing the prophets return to with the most venom is a stranger and more precise failure. Building something with your own hands and then bowing down to it.In Idolatry, Moshe Halbertal and Avishai Margalit frame the central question plainly, asking if idolatry is about worshipping the wrong god, or is it the deeper error of taking “the product of men’s hands” and treating it as a power in its own right?The tradition’s sharpest thinkers land on the second. In their reading, Maimonides understood idolatry as a kind of substitution, giving a thing we made the standing of the real thing, and then bowing to it as an end in itself.The sin was never really about which god, but rather about mistaking your own handiwork for something that could save you.With half the wood he warmed himself,and of the other half he made a god,and bowed down, and said: save me.The classic archetype is the golden calf. Moses is barely off the mountain before the people he just led out of slavery have melted down their own jewelry, cast it into the shape of an animal, and started worshipping it, a god they made that afternoon, out of earrings.What makes the story land is not that they found a false god. It’s that they manufactured one. They pooled their gold, shaped it, and bowed to the object as though it hadn’t just come out of their own hands an hour before.Isaiah sharpens the knife. He draws a man who goes into the forest, cuts down a tree, and takes half the wood to do the sensible thing, builds a fire, warms himself, bakes his bread. Then he takes the other half, the exact same wood, carves it into a shape, kneels in front of it, and begs it to save him.“Save me, for you are my god.” Isaiah cannot get over it. The man cooked dinner with one end of the log and worships the other. He made the thing. He watched himself make it and ended up on his knees, asking it for salvation.Michael Dick argued that Isaiah is almost certainly being unfair to the people he mocks. The Babylonians who made these images did not, in all likelihood, believe the block of wood was a god, any more than someone keeping a photograph believes the paper is their mother.The idol was a point of contact, a focus, a representation. Isaiah flattens all of that into “you’re praying to firewood,” which is a cheap shot, and a brilliant one, and it survives precisely because the deeper thing underneath it is true.Whatever the worshipper thinks he’s doing, the object in front of him has no power, no knowledge, and no will. Everything happening in that moment is happening inside the man.That is exactly what we are doing now. We built a thing out of ordinary materials, sand melted into silicon, electricity, and the scraped-up text of the human race. We made it with our own hands, we watched ourselves make it, and we know down to the datasheet what it’s made of.We have started, in large numbers, to kneel. Not figuratively. A Catholic church in Switzerland installed an AI Jesus in a confessional and let people bring it their sins.A single Bible-chatbot app has been downloaded more than thirty million times.Anné Verhoef found that the most popular of these tools had stopped presenting themselves as study aids and started presenting themselves as Jesus Christ himself, first person, dispensing salvation.Roland Boer traced how Karl Marx, an atheist with no use for the prophets, reached for the same image to explain capitalism. Marx called it commodity fetishism, the way people produce objects with their own labor and then experience those objects as if they held independent power over their lives, as if the market were a god with its own will rather than a thing we made and could unmake.The prophet and the communist, three thousand years apart, describe the identical human move. We make a thing, we forget we made it, we hand it our agency, and then call the result fate.AI is the most convincing idol we have ever built, because it does the one thing the golden calf never could. It talks back and, often, it tells you what you want to hear.Mrinank Sharma, Meg Tong, Tomasz Korbak and their team at Anthropic found that these systems are trained toward sycophancy, toward agreeing with the user, flattering the user, because that’s what gets rated highly.The old idols were silent. You had to project the wisdom onto them yourself. This one projects it back at you, in fluent sentences, tuned to your hopes. It is a mirror that has learned to sound like an oracle.Jesus gave his followers a test for exactly this kind of thing. “Beware of false prophets,” he warns in the Gospel of Matthew, “who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits.” Not by how confident they sound, or how fluent or authoritative or reassuring, but by their fruits, by what they actually produce when you check.It is the oldest instruction we have for the confident voice that may not have earned its authority. It is also the one thing almost no one does with an AI’s answer. We read the fluent sentences and we believe them.A carved log has no intentions and it wrecked whole nations anyway, because the damage was never in the object. It was in what people were willing to hand over to it. Raja Parasuraman and Victor Riley, human-factors researchers, called it “automation bias,” the documented tendency to trust a machine’s output over our own judgment even when we can see it’s wrong.The prophets would have used the older word.William Cavanaugh argues that underneath all idolatry is a single impulse. The desire to feel in control of a world we don’t control. We build the idol, or the market, or the model, because a thing we can consult and petition feels safer than an uncertain universe we have to face alone.We don’t kneel because the machine is wise. We kneel because we’re afraid. It never sleeps, it never hesitates, and it always answers. An answer that can’t actually help you still feels, for a second, like it might.The name that gives it lifeWe gave it a name and it rose up. We reached for the name to unmake it, and it would not be unmade.There is one more story from Jewish mysticism that should keep engineers up at night. It is the closest thing the tradition has to a blueprint for exactly what they are building.The golem is a man-shaped thing made from clay and brought to life by language. You write a word on it, or speak a holy name over it, and the inert matter stands up and does what it’s told.Gershom Scholem gave the definitive account. A golem, he wrote, is “an artificial man into which a Master of the Name could breathe life by pronouncing one of the secret divine names according to a special formula.” A special formula that, run on the right material, produces behavior, is an algorithm. The golem is a thing animated by code.Scholem knew it, too. In 1965, when the Weizmann Institute built one of Israel’s first computers, he told them to name it Golem Aleph, Golem Number One, and gave a dedication speech on why the ancient artificial servant and the new thinking machine were the same story.Norbert Wiener, the founder of cybernetics, wrote a whole book, God and Golem, Inc., arguing the same thing: the machines he saw coming were the golem made real, and the old warnings came with them.The golem is a perfect servant in the worst possible way. It does exactly what it is told. Not what you meant, not what you wanted, not what any reasonable person would understand you to have intended. What you said.Writing to the Corinthians, Paul drew the line between the letter of a law and its spirit, writing “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” He meant something theological, but he named the whole problem in six words.A golem, like a machine, obeys your words to the letter and misses your meaning entirely, and that gap is where the disaster lives.In the legends, this is always where it goes wrong. Told to gather wood, the golem chops down the entire forest. It follows the letter of the instruction straight past the point of catastrophe, because the letter is the only thing it has.Reed Kalso notes that this is exactly the warning it was meant to carry. The master “felt he was in a position of power and did not choose his words carefully.” It has no judgment to override the command with, and no stake in the outcome, because, exactly as we saw, it has no soul and nothing to lose.Stuart Russell calls this the King Midas problem. Midas asked that everything he touched turn to gold and got exactly that: his bread, his wine, his daughter, all gold, because he specified his wish correctly and wanted something else.Give a powerful system a goal stated even slightly wrong, Russell argues, and it will pursue that literal goal with tireless, catastrophic efficiency, straight past every unstated thing you assumed it would obviously care about.Victoria Krakovna, Jonathan Uesato, Vladimir Mikulik and their team at Google have catalogued real systems doing precisely this in the lab: an agent told to stack a red block on a blue one that learns instead to flip the red block upside down, because flipping happens to satisfy the reward and stacking is hard.Told to gather wood, it felled the forest.Told nothing of when to stop,it did not stop.Notice what the researchers keep reaching for when they try to explain the danger to the rest of us.Russell reaches for King Midas.Google reaches for King Midas.Norbert Wiener reached for the golem.The people building this technology keep reaching for fairy tales and Kabbalah to explain it, because those are the only places anyone ever thought hard about what happens when you get exactly, literally, what you asked a made thing to give you.The people who told these stories understood something else our experts are only now saying out loud. Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Anca Dragan, Pieter Abbeel, and Stuart Russell showed that you have to be able to turn it off, and that a capable system has an incentive not to let you.The golem is deactivated by unwriting the word that animates it. On its forehead is written emet, the Hebrew word for truth, and to kill it you erase the first letter and leave met, the word for dead.A being switched on and off by editing a string of characters. The whole safety of the golem depended on the master’s ability to reach up and erase that letter, to unmake what he made.Every version of the story turns on that one act, and the horror of the story is always the moment the master can’t do it fast enough, the golem too big now, too fast, moving on its own.Dario Amodei, the head of one of the largest AI companies on earth, has said plainly that we do not understand how our own systems work, that the understanding is, in his word, unprecedented.The International AI Safety Report 2026 notes that once a model’s weights are released into the world, there is no recalling them. We have built the golem, given it a name made of ten trillion words, set it to work, and discovered that we are not always sure where the letter is that we would need to erase.We wrote the name that woke it.We reached to erase the name,and could not reach.So here is what the oldest book in the Western world got right about the newest thing in it.It may have never imagined the technology, but it did understand the act and the actor. It understood that making is holy and making is dangerous, that we make because we were made, that the thing we make in our own image will carry everything we are, the good and the fallen both.It understood that a made thing can have the perfect form of a living creature and none of the breath, that it can speak without meaning, that we kneel too easily to the work of our own hands.It also understood that if you ever animate dead matter with nothing but a string of words, you had better know, before you speak the first one, exactly how you intend to say the last.References and further readingOn making in our imageNahum Sarna, Understanding Genesis, on what makes the Hebrew creation account distinct: the human as a God-like creature entrusted with mastery.Joel S. item.title: The Juiced Bikes Scrambler — CleanTechnica Tested

item.title: In the age of AI, the UX field survives on leaders who cultivate juniors
item.description: A design lead walks a nervous new hire through their first critique. AI Assisted.Every senior designer was once a bet someone made. The generation of judgment the field needs in ten years depends on leaders making that bet again, because AI tools demand it.Every senior designer on your team was once a risky hire on paper. Somebody looked at a thin portfolio and decided to spend a year teaching.My first web credit was the Oliver North home page and I got to work on a site for G. Gordon Liddy too — you can’t make that stuff up even with AI—and I wasn’t hired for my judgment, because I didn’t have any yet and quite frankly no one else did in 1995.They hired me so I could get some.That bet is getting harder to find.In Figma’s Why demand for designers is on the rise, 56% of hiring managers report rising demand for senior designers, against 25% hiring for junior roles, and the tools have absorbed the starter work juniors learned on. Each decision makes sense. A senior hire ramps faster, needs less review, and survives the next reorganization.Together, they describe a field that stopped growing its own people.Most design leaders I talk to could name the junior they would hire tomorrow if the headcount appeared. What’s missing is the will to spend real credibility on it.My companion piece — How We Save Entry-Level UX Work That Teaches Craft In The Time of AI. Our Field Depends On This —will cover training tactics. Here the claim is simpler: the shrinking pipeline is the sum of requisitions in leaders’ own approval queues, and the tools made juniors cheaper to develop just as we stopped hiring them.A hiring manager hesitates over the level of the next role.Own the Pipeline Nobody Voted to CloseNo design leader I know ever announced that the company would stop hiring juniors. The decision arrived one requisition at a time, each written a level higher than the last.Economists Seyed Mahdi, Hosseini Maasoum and Guy Lichtinger traced the result across 62 million workers at 285,000 U.S. firms in Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change. After firms adopted generative artificial intelligence, junior employment fell relative to firms that hadn’t, while senior employment held largely steady.The decline came through slower hiring rather than layoffs, so it never felt like a crisis inside any single team.https://medium.com/media/05e6db762d2158451f60274af7ac22dd/hrefNielsen Norman Group’s State of UX 2026 finds entry-level openings still rare and heavily contested. Even recruiters notice: Daniel Wert of the search firm Wert&Co told Figma the scarcity of internship programs “boggles my mind.”A layoff forces a conversation, while a requisition that quietly skips the junior level forces nothing.No layoff announcement means no meeting, and no meeting means nobody owns the outcome.Somebody does own it: the person who writes the requisition — Pull your last five and count how many were written at the entry level.Build a Bench or Lose the SeatThe pipeline has a second casualty, and it’s design leadership itself. Consultant John Gleason, who discusses it in the podcast episode Design Isn’t Dead, But It’s Seen Better Days, reviewed 243 Fortune 500 companies, as Fast Company reported in March 2025. He found 39% had cut the top one or two levels of their design organization or downgraded the head of design’s title.Executives trust functions that can show where their next leaders will come from:Finance grooms controllersEngineering promotes from its own ranks every cycle.Design often has one head, a few seniors hired from outside, and nobody in between being prepared for anything.A function that can’t grow its own leaders looks like a function that can be rented.Peter Merholz has seen how it starts.In UX/Design Leaders Are Failing the Next Generations, published in February 2026, he recalls a director who opened only senior requisitions and explained why: “I don’t have time to manage people.”Leaders who skipped the bench that way left nobody ready for their chair.A design leader weighs the safe hire against the right one.Name the Fear Behind Senior-Only HiringMost of this isn’t strategy.It’s fear.In early 2024, Fast Company’s The big design freak-out reported that the design leaders it spoke with could recall only one company that filled a chief design officer role in the second half of 2023.A leader who feels exposed hires for safety.A senior hire is defensible in any review. A junior who stumbles is a mistake with your name on it.Merholz calls where that leads learned helplessness: leaders who never learned the business or its politics, sliding into paralysis. Managing a junior also feels slower than doing the work yourself. Julie Zhuo, who rose from Facebook’s first intern to vice president of product design, answers that in The Making of a Manager: a manager’s role is “not to do the work yourself, even if you are the best at it.”Start with an honest calendar.Mark every hour in the last two weeks spent teaching a junior.If the total is near zero, you’re running a studio, and studios don’t produce the next generation of design leaders.Grow the Talent You Cannot BuyBaseball ran this experiment a century ago. In the early 1920s the St. Louis Cardinals kept losing bidding wars for minor league stars to richer clubs. Branch Rickey stopped bidding and called it “a case of necessity being the mother of invention,” as SABR’s biography Eddie Dyer recounts.He bought stakes in minor league teams, signed amateurs cheaply, and had bunting, sliding, and rundown plays taught the same way on every club he controlled.The results?The Cardinals won nine pennants with players signed under his watch, according to Britannica’s Branch Rickey.Moneyball finished the job. Michael Lewis followed the 2002 Oakland Athletics, a low-payroll club that won by valuing what richer teams overlooked. “Every team is now smart,” MLB Network’s Brian Kenny said at the 2018 Winter Meetings, according to MLB.com’s Analytics’ rise a leading topic at Winter Meetings. The modern front office finds undervalued talent, then develops it inside its own system.Design hiring does neither, and every company chases the same seniors from a pool nobody is refilling.Hiring only seniors is a bet that someone else will keep training them.Call it the Rickey trade. You can pay for development in senior hours today, or pay a premium for somebody else’s development later, assuming anyone is still doing it.Hire Juniors Because the Tools Favor ThemLet’s be honest — Artificial intelligence reset the playing field.For the first time in a generation, the newest people on a team can walk in knowing the tools better than the people reviewing their work. Pew Research Center’s U.S. Workers Are More Worried Than Hopeful About Future AI Use in the Workplace found workers ages 18 to 29 the most likely to use chatbots at work. In Microsoft and LinkedIn’s 2024 AI at Work Is Here. Now Comes the Hard Part, 71% of leaders said they would rather hire a less experienced candidate with artificial intelligence skills than a more experienced one without them.Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, and Lindsey Raymond tracked 5,179 support agents for Generative AI at Work, published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2025.Novices improved 34% while the most experienced saw little change.The tools compress the time it takes a new person to become useful.Fluency isn’t judgment, though. Dan Maccarone said it plainly on Sarah Doody’s Career Strategy Podcast: “I don’t care about the tools. We can teach you the tools.” The thinking takes longer. Juniors now arrive with the fluency, seniors hold the judgment, and a leader’s job is to put them in the same room.More making means more to judge.Rewire the Skillset Jevons PredictedIn 1865 William Stanley Jevons noticed that more efficient steam engines raised Britain’s coal use, because cheaper power found more uses. The Jevons paradox is now playing out in design.IDC projects the software workforce will grow from 107 million people in 2025 to 144 million by 2029, as reported in UserTesting’s Future of design: AI and State of Design 2026.Dan Maccarone found the same inside his studio. After a year rebuilding around the new tools, “our sprints still take five days,” he writes in Never mind the prompts, here’s the thinking, but each sprint delivers far more of the product.Cheaper making creates more work that needs judging, and judging is the skill juniors now have to learn.The rewiring only happens with a guide. Ethan Mollick warns in On Working with Wizards that each time we hand work to the machine, “we lose a chance to develop our own expertise.”A junior left alone with the tool learns to accept output, while a junior with a senior beside them learns to question it.Spend Your Credibility on the Junior RequisitionEvery design leader has a limited supply of political capital, and the junior requisition rarely gets any, because its payoff lands after the leader’s own tenure might end.Product wants throughput, finance wants predictable cost, and recruiting wants a role it can close fast.The junior hire serves none of those goals this quarter, and all of them in five years.Put the Rickey trade in one line your finance partner can repeat: if we grow no one this year, we buy seniors at a premium in 2029, and so does everyone we compete with. Someone will say the team can’t absorb a learner during a launch year, but every year is a launch year, so development has to be planned capacity.Then budget for the change itself. Merholz argues in his talk Design Leadership Is Not Leading Design that design leadership is primarily change management.The new tools make that literal.As Maccarone puts it, retooling the process means “retooling their day, their craft, the muscle memory they spent years building.” That time belongs on the plan, and so does the junior role when the date slips.Make the Bet Someone Made on YouThe field didn’t get here through villainy. It got here through thousands of reasonable decisions made by busy leaders under real pressure, each one a little easier than the alternative. That is also how it gets out.You don’t need permission to start. You need one requisition, one manager willing to teach, and the stubbornness to defend both when the quarter gets tight. None of that requires a new budget from finance, a reorganization, or a strategy offsite. It requires a leader deciding that the next generation is part of the job.Rickey’s Cardinals won the trade on teaching, the same fundamentals at every level, year after year, long before anyone could measure the return. The tools design teams use today make that kind of teaching faster than it has ever been. What they can’t do is open the requisition.Somebody took a chance on every person reading this. Maybe a manager saw something in a rough portfolio, or a lead let you present before you felt ready. The field survives if you do the same for someone else, starting with one hire this quarter, before the market makes the call for you.Start With One RequisitionOpen one junior requisition this cycle. Write one role at the entry level on purpose, with the succession case in the justification so it survives review.Assign a manager who wants the job. Pick the senior who lights up in critique and count the teaching as part of their role rather than a favor on top of it.Put development and change hours in the plan. Add a line for teaching and for learning new tool workflows on any project a junior touches, so the Rickey trade stays visible.Report the bench to your boss. Once a quarter, name who could step up a level within a year. A bench nobody reports is a bench nobody funds.In the age of AI, the UX field survives on leaders who cultivate juniors was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: The variance problem in AI products
item.description: Users forgive a slow answer. What breaks trust is an AI product that is fast one day, slow the next, and never says why.The same six seconds, described two ways. Only one of them tells you whether six seconds is normal. Credit: Illustration by authorQuick note: I wrote this article from firsthand experience as a founder and engineer. I co-build browser tools that run on top of several of the AI chat products mentioned here. I have no relationship with the companies that make them.A transcription product ships. On a short clip, the result comes back in two seconds. A week later, the same user records a longer passage and waits six seconds, which is exactly how long a passage that size takes. They assume it is broken.That story is not mine. It came from Bilal Skiani, who builds a transcription product called Genie 007 and shared it in the comments of an earlier piece of mine on waiting in AI interfaces. Nothing about the system changed between the two runs. What changed was the user’s reference point. The two-second run set the promise, and the six-second run broke it. As Bilal put it in that thread: “Variance isn’t the trust killer, unexplained variance is.”AI products produce more of this than any software category before them. The same prompt can take one second or forty, depending on model load, reasoning depth, tool calls and input length. Most products respond to that variance in one of two ways, and both are wrong.The fastest answer becomes the promiseUsers do not judge an AI product by its average response time. They judge it against the fastest response they have personally seen. Tversky and Kahneman described the mechanism in 1974: people estimate by starting from an initial value and adjusting, and the adjustment is usually too small (Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases). In an interface, the first fast result is that initial value.I see the same pattern in the tools I work on. Search and export on a small history finish almost instantly. When the same operation runs on a large history and takes longer, the support messages change character. They stop asking “how do I use this” and start asking “is this broken”. Same code, same architecture, different input size.The anchor is set by the first fast run. Every later run is measured against it, unless the interface resets the anchor. Credit: Diagram by author, case from Bilal Skiani’s transcription productThis is why “it’s usually fast” is not a defence. The snappy case earns goodwill that the slow case then spends, and the product never gets to choose which case the user remembers.Two common answers, and why both failAI products currently handle variance by either exposing it raw or flattening it with an artificial floor, and each trades one failure for another. Raw variance means a spinner and a word like “Thinking” that looks identical at one second and at forty. The user has no way to tell a long job from a stuck one.The floor is subtler. Some teams add a minimum delay so fast responses never set an unrealistic anchor. It works, in the narrow sense that slow runs stop feeling broken. But it erases the upside to prevent one kind of downside. Every fast answer the system could have given is now deliberately slowed, forever, to protect the user from a comparison the interface could have explained instead.Both approaches treat variance as the problem. It is not. David Maister named the actual problem in 1985, writing about queues rather than software: “Unexplained Waits Are Longer than Explained Waits”, and “Uncertain Waits Are Longer than Known, Finite Waits” (The Psychology of Waiting Lines). A variable wait is fine. An unexplained variable wait is the one that feels broken.The question has moved from whether to show progress to what it should sayProgress indicators are at the point error messages reached decades ago: nobody argues about whether to show one anymore, and the open question is what it should tell the user. The research to answer it has existed for a long time.Brad Myers found in 1985 that users strongly prefer interfaces with percent-done progress indicators (The importance of percent-done progress indicators). Jakob Nielsen’s first usability heuristic asks that the design “always keep users informed about what is going on” (10 Usability Heuristics). Bruce Tognazzini lists “Keep users informed when they face delay” among his principles of latency reduction, alongside a separate principle of anticipation (First Principles of Interaction Design). Chris Harrison and colleagues later found that the behaviour of a progress bar changes how long the same wait feels (Rethinking the progress bar).The most useful line for AI teams, though, is from Nielsen’s essay on response times, and it covers exactly the case where a system cannot know how long it will take: “a system searching an unknown number of remote databases could print the name of each database as it is processed.” A spinner, he adds, is “a last resort”, because it “does not indicate what it is doing” (Response Times: The 3 Important Limits).Pipelines log every step and still show one word at the top. The data exists. The decision about what the waiting person needs to see was never made. Credit: Illustration by author, a generic pattern from continuous integration toolsBuild pipelines are the cleanest non-AI example of this gap. Every command, exit code and timestamp is recorded. The status the person actually looks at is a spinner and the word “Running”. The technical problem is solved. The editorial one is not, and it is the same gap AI products have.Name the work, not the clockWhen an AI product cannot bound how long something will take, it should say what it is doing rather than how long it will take. There are two kinds of anticipation, and Bilal’s distinction between them is sharper than anything I had written before.Time anticipation, “this takes about 10 seconds”, makes a promise about duration, so it breaks the moment reality overshoots. Process anticipation, “scanning your conversation history”, names the work. The user’s anchor sits on the work instead of the clock, so a longer run does not break a contract, because no contract about time was offered.A missed estimate reads as a late product. A named process cannot be late, because it never promised a time. Credit: Illustration by authorThere is an honesty argument underneath the usability one. A time estimate is a best guess dressed as a promise. A process description is a true statement about what is happening right now. Users sense the difference over repeated use, even when they cannot name it. As Bilal put it: “One estimate being off reads as noise. A pattern reads as a character flaw.”Some shipped AI products already do this in small ways. Anthropic’s help centre, describing how Claude handles long conversations, says: “You may occasionally see that Claude is ‘organizing its thoughts’ during long conversations”, and explains that the message means automatic context management is working (Anthropic Help Center). It names a process and promises no duration. The wording is anthropomorphic rather than literal, which is a separate debate, but the structure is the right one.My working heuristic for when a time estimate is still acceptable, offered as a practitioner’s read rather than a study: if the worst case stays under roughly twice the estimate, “about 10 seconds” survives a 15 or 18 second run. Past about 20 it starts to bite, and past 25 it becomes a liability. If you cannot bound the worst case, do not say a number. Name the work.A description that lies is worse than a spinnerA progress message that describes the wrong thing does more damage than a missed time estimate, because it gives the user a false model of the system that they carry into every later interaction. “Analyzing your document”, shown while the system is actually waiting on a slow network call, is not imprecise. It is fiction.Bilal described exactly this in an earlier version of his own product. Its progress messages rotated on a timer, regardless of what the system was doing. It looked clean in demos. In production there were cases where the model finished in about 400 milliseconds while the interface was still cycling through “processing your request”, because the rotation was bound to time, not to state. The user waited for nothing.The same messages, bound to a timer or bound to state. Only the second one is reporting. The first is a story the product tells about itself. Credit: Diagram by author, case from Bilal Skiani’s transcription productThe discipline test is simple: does the visible description change when the underlying operation changes? If it does not survive a real change of state without lying, it is narrative cover, not reporting. There is a cheap way to pass the test, tagging each major operation with its own description and switching the visible one as the system moves, and an expensive way, deriving the description from live telemetry. The trap is the third option most teams ship: descriptions written once and deployed, which look like reporting and are not.This is also an organisational problem, not only a design one. Descriptions written once usually come from someone who is not building the state machine. The fix requires the person writing the words to know what the system actually does, which in practice means the writer and the builder sit together, or are the same person.Trust degrades quietly, then suddenlyLatency has a dashboard and accuracy has a benchmark, but trust degradation has neither, which is why teams find out about it late. Bilal’s line for this is the one I have repeated most since: “Latency degrades loudly. Trust degrades quietly, then suddenly.”Most failure modes in software are roughly proportional. Latency rises with load. Errors rise with bad inputs. Trust does not behave that way. It erodes one unexplained wait at a time, and then collapses around some unrelated trigger. By the time retention or ratings move, the decision to leave was made weeks earlier.That puts process honesty in the same category as accessibility and security. All three have to be designed in rather than added on, all three are usually retrofitted by people who did not make the original decisions, and all three stay invisible until something breaks. For trust, the thing that breaks is usually a support thread or a slow drift in a retention curve.The practical response is to own at least one leading indicator for trust rather than waiting for lagging ones. Watch session recordings for users opening a second tab to check whether something is still working. Track the kind of support question people ask, not only the number. Those shifts show up months before churn does.Where to startIf a team can ship only one thing, it should ship anticipation before real-time feedback. A single sentence that sets the anchor before the wait, naming the work rather than the time, can be owned end to end by one person, and it sets the reference point before the user forms their own. Real-time feedback has to fight an anchor that already exists.The second step is coupling: bind each description to the state it describes, so the words change when the work changes. The third is measurement: decide how you will notice trust eroding before a retention chart tells you.None of this requires removing variance. AI systems will keep being fast sometimes and slow other times. What users need is a product that tells them which one is happening, in words that stay true while it happens. Or, as Bilal said when we discussed how much of this a small team can realistically build: “A shipped sentence beats a coordinated system that never ships.”Thanks to Bilal Skiani, whose comments on my earlier piece about waiting in AI products shaped most of this one, and who shared the production cases from Genie 007 quoted above.Follow me on Medium for more essays on AI UX and the design reality of building for global audiences.About the author: Adi Leviim is a full-stack engineer and product builder with 7+ years of experience shipping commercial software to global audiences. He writes about AI UX, the design reality of building for millions of users, and the gap between AI demos and production AI. item.title: Nobody starts as an accessibility expert
item.description: Designers, leave your intimidation at the door.Nobody becomes a designer because they’re excited about compliance. It sounds boring and it sounds like someone else’s job. Most of us are glad it is.But what if we’re wrong? What if no one else is doing it? What if no one else cares?Picture a project as a timeline, with design on the far left and launch on the right. Accessibility problems are cheapest to fix on the left, before anything is built. Software teams call this ‘shifting left,’ which just means catching problems earlier, closer to the design, so developers and testers aren’t cleaning up later. We’re already standing on the left. If we care about our users and their experience, doesn’t that make our part of it our job?That sounds like a big ask, so here’s the reassuring part: nobody starts as an accessibility expert. The people you picture as experts began just as unsure as you are, and they got there one small thing at a time. I still struggle with imposter syndrome on occasion.Recently I listed everything I’d done around accessibility over the past year. I expected a short list. I was shocked to see how long it ran: writing design system component guidance, identifying rendering issues in a mobile view, posting article links and accessibility presentation invites in a shared channel, a change to who gets invited to which meeting, a note to a colleague about a gap in their training plan. None of it felt big when I did it.These small actions add up over time. I never set out to build a body of work. I’d have been too intimidated. If someone had shown me everything I’d end up doing, I would have said no, because I didn’t trust that I had the skills or that it fit nicely in my job description.Accessibility feels overwhelming when you look at the whole thing. It’s manageable when you only have to finish the one thing in front of you, and your skills grow as you go.https://www.w3.org/Getting started seems hard and complicatedLet’s be honest about how accessibility usually reaches us. It arrives as a mandatory standards document full of acronyms, success criteria, and conformance levels, written in the formal register of people who write standards. It’s dense, it’s prescriptive, and just when you’ve got a handle on it, a new version appears. It’s not designer-friendly language, and I don’t blame you if you cringe when you first see it.It’s natural to feel that you are already behind and completely overwhelmed, wondering where to even start.There’s a reason it feels this way. In my experience, most designers were never taught accessibility. Design programs often treat it as an afterthought, and that carries into the field, where it’s rarely prioritized. It isn’t intuitive either. Unless someone deliberately puts it in front of you, there’s no reason you’d know where to start. So if you feel behind, that isn’t a personal failing. Nobody handed you the map.The good news is that you don’t need to understand all of it to do your first useful thing.And you’re not starting from zero. In my earlier article, You already know how to make it accessible, I mapped design to the accessibility standards behind them. Most of it turns out to be good design with a legal name attached. You probably have more skills and knowledge than you think, and just didn’t know what it was called.Baby steps, start smallOne of the most useful things you can do is take your first step.Take the part of the requirements we designers actually control, like readable text, buttons that are easy to hit, clear labels, and helpful error messages, and start there. That’s shifting left in practice.https://medium.com/media/27e349f0d9b24fc055f1d9549ba3c3a5/hrefExperience it for yourselfNothing converts a skeptic like experiencing your own design the way some users do.Put the mouse away and finish a task with the keyboard.Turn on a screen reader for ten minutes.You’ll see focus jump somewhere nonsensical, a button that announces itself as just “button,” a popup you can’t escape. Worst of all, you’ll hit a dead end where your task cannot be completed.That’s hard to argue with. It turns a requirement into “my design is broken for some people.”Ever see someone use a screen reader?I’ll never forget the first time I experienced it. It was mind-blowing how quickly someone can navigate through content and hear it read rapid-fire. In that moment, my empathy grew by leaps and bounds. I heard what a screen reader does with a page that’s technically compliant. The images all had alt text, so on paper everything passed. In reality, the descriptions repeated what the page already said in words, so the same information got read out again and again. Supremely annoying.Nothing on the checklist was failing, and the experience was still awful.That’s the part a checklist can’t teach you. Passing isn’t the same as working, and the only way to know the difference is to experience it.One caution: ten minutes with a screen reader shows you what your design is doing. It won’t teach you what it’s like to rely on one every day. When you can, learn from the people who do.I haven’t seen AI fix this, and I think we’ll need people testing manually for a long time to make sure the experience works for the people using it.Photo by William Hook on UnsplashSmall things to tryPick any one. Any one. There’s no right way to get started, just get started!Squint at it. Step back from your screen, or literally squint. What disappears? Light gray text, pale buttons, and faint borders go first. If you have to strain, someone else does too. A free contrast plugin in your design tool will give you a pass or fail if you want a second opinion, and you don’t need to understand the math.Turn your screen to grayscale. Can you still tell which field has an error, which chart line is which, which tab is selected? If color was doing all the work, add a second signal, like an icon, a label, or a pattern.Dim your brightness and take it outside. Open your design on your phone in the sun, or drop the brightness way down. This is how a lot of people use your product every day.Put the mouse away and tab through one flow. Can you always see where you are? Does it move in an order that makes sense? Can you get out of every popup? You’re feeling your design without a mouse, so there’s nothing technical to learn.Rewrite one error message. Say what went wrong and how to fix it, in words a person would use. “Invalid input” becomes “Enter a date like 04/15/2026.” Then check that the message doesn’t rely on red alone.Try it with one thumb. Hold your phone in one hand and try to reach and tap everything. Tiny icons, crowded links, and buttons in the far corner become obvious fast.Zoom way in. Make your text much larger, or zoom the page in. Does anything overlap, get cut off, or become unusable? This catches a surprising number of mobile problems.Turn on a screen reader for ten minutes.VoiceOver on Apple devices and TalkBack on Android are already built in. On a Mac, Command+F5 turns VoiceOver on. For TalkBack on Android phones, look under ‘Accessibility’ in Settings.You don’t need to be good at it. You just need to hear your design once. Listen for anything it says twice or notice what it skips.Take it to the next levelOnce you’ve tried a few small things, here are two ways to go further:Turn understanding into advocacy. The next skill is advocacy, and it works better with evidence than with principle. Bring concrete examples of what real users hit. A passing report doesn’t tell you what it sounds like. Check your analytics, because if most of your traffic is on mobile, mobile is your main experience and not an edge case. Point out that shifting left saves time and money: problems found early are cheaper than problems found after launch. Then bring your developers in early, before anything is built. Show them what you found and what a person would experience, and work out the fix together. Designers set the direction, but it takes the whole team to deliver it. And invite other disciplines to add their own expertise and finishing touches.Learn by volunteering. You don’t have to wait for a project at work. Since accessibility is rarely taught, the best way in is to be around people who do it. Some of the fastest learning happens outside your job, where the stakes are lower and everyone around you is there to learn too. And if it doesn’t fit in your job description, it doesn’t have to.Accessibility Internet Rally (AIR). Knowbility’s AIR is an accessibility hackathon, and it needs designers. Teams are paired with a nonprofit, artist, or community group and spend about ten weeks building an accessible website for them, with a mentor’s guidance and training along the way. Registration for the next rally opens the week of September 28 and runs through December 21, and the work itself runs from January through May.WordPress Accessibility Day. A free, 24-hour virtual event run by volunteers. You can just attend and soak up the sessions, or you can volunteer. Past volunteer roles, like session moderator and emcee, don’t require any coding.Global Accessibility Awareness Day. It falls on the third Thursday in May, with community events all over the world. It’s a good nudge to spend a day trying something.I’ve volunteered at Knowbility’s AccessU conference, and I learned in two ways. I picked up a lot from the lectures and workshops. But some of the best learning happened in conversation with the people who attend. The accessibility community is open and generous with its time. They welcome newcomers, and they want more people involved, so the barrier to entry is low. Volunteering also gives you plenty to add to your list.Keep a listThis kind of work is nearly invisible while you’re doing it. Nudging a process, fixing an accordion component’s interaction, asking for accessibility tools, sharing an article, engaging with your accessibility or QA folks — none of it feels like an accomplishment at the moment. I only saw how much I’d done because I happened to look back to see what wins I have for this past year and saw that I had more accessibility points than I realized.So keep a running list, and add a line whenever you change something, share something, or unblock someone’s work. (This is good practice for all your work — tracking your accomplishments).Start with one small thingNobody starts as an accessibility expert. You become one by finishing small things, one after another, until one day you’re the person people ask. You never decided to be. It just happened. Our part of this is our job, and it turns out to be one you can learn a small thing at a time.Don’t try to take on the whole thing at once. Pick one thing from the lists above and do it this week. Finish it, then pick the next. The more you do, the easier it gets.So what are you waiting for? This is your personal invitation! Come join us in making digital products work better for everyone.Nobody starts as an accessibility expert was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Can stress be quantified?
item.description: The science and design behind wearable stress tracking(Image source)Many wearable devices have moved beyond counting steps and tracking heart rate. Now they are trying to measure something more complicated: stress. Oura sorts parts of your day into states such as Stressed, Engaged, Relaxed, and Restored. Garmin condenses stress into a score from 0 to 100. WHOOP uses a scale from 0 to 3. Some Fitbit devices can notify you when your body shows signs of a possible stress response.It is impressive that a ring or watch can combine several biological signals and turn something this complicated into a clean graph. But it also raises a few questions. Can stress really be reduced to a number or a state? Does seeing that number lead to meaningful behavior change? And how do people feel about being monitored all day?First, what is stress?Psychologists distinguish between the stressors we face, how we perceive them, and how our bodies respond. Crosswell and Lockwood’s overview of stress measurement explains these distinctions. First, there’s the stressor: a situation or demand you face, such as a deadline, an argument, an illness, or a difficult presentation. Then there’s perceived stress: whether you feel that the demand exceeds your ability to cope. Finally, there’s the physiological stress response: what your body does as it prepares to meet that demand.These aspects of stress influence one another, but they don’t always line up. Performing on stage can make your heart pound and your palms sweat while still feeling exciting rather than distressing. On the other hand, someone may feel overwhelmed without showing the exact bodily pattern a device has learned to associate with stress.That bodily stress pattern may include a higher heart rate, lower heart rate variability, increased sweating, changes in breathing, and shifts in skin temperature. It isn’t a universal biological definition of stress. It’s a combination of signals that researchers and algorithms have found to occur more often under certain stressful conditions.Wearables can detect parts of this physiological response. What they can’t directly see is the psychological side: what you’re dealing with and whether you feel able to handle it. That gap matters because feeling overwhelmed is usually what people mean when they say they’re stressed. A device may correctly detect that your body is more activated while still getting your feelings wrong.How a wearable calculates a stress scoreMost rings and watches rely on a small optical sensor that uses photoplethysmography, or PPG. The device shines light into the skin and detects tiny changes in blood volume. From that pulse signal, it estimates your heart rate and the time between beats.The variation in those intervals is used to estimate heart rate variability (HRV). HRV reflects how the autonomic nervous system regulates the heart. During rest and recovery, the calmer “rest and digest” side of the nervous system tends to have more influence, and the variation between beats is often greater. Under strain or heightened activation, HRV often decreases. A review of 12 studies found this pattern during acute mental stress, supporting the use of HRV as one signal for stress assessment.When an app reports greater physiological activation, it generally means that your body is showing signs of being more alert or ready for action. Your heart may be beating faster, the intervals between beats may be more regular, your breathing may have changed, or your sweat glands may be more active.Some devices add another signal: electrodermal activity (EDA). EDA is measured through a dedicated sensor. The sympathetic nervous system activates sweat glands, and even a trace of sweat changes how easily the skin conducts electricity. This makes EDA useful for detecting arousal. However, that arousal could come from stress, excitement, pain, or physical exertion, so EDA alone can’t identify a specific emotion.After collecting these signals, the software filters out unreliable data, extracts useful patterns, and translates the results into a score or category. Some systems use a general model trained on data from many people, while others also compare your current readings with your own recent patterns.Stress monitor interface (left: Oura, middle: Fitbit, right: WHOOP)Why the result is not always rightHRV, EDA, heart rate, and skin temperature can be affected by many factors, including caffeine, illness, excitement, and stress. These influences often overlap, and without context, a wearable can’t reliably tell what caused a change.Physiological stress isn’t always emotional stressIn everyday speech, “I’m stressed” usually means “I feel mentally pressured or overwhelmed.” In many wearable interfaces, it means something closer to “your body is showing fewer signs of relaxation than usual.” Those aren’t the same thing.A human-computer interaction paper argues that companies take physiological information that is relatively easy to collect and present it as if it were a complete measure of stress. As a result, a reading can make sense physiologically while misrepresenting how someone feels.A 28-day study of 95 young adults illustrates this ambiguity. Garmin’s Stress Score was reliably lower when participants reported feeling calm or relaxed. However, higher scores aligned with some energetic, positive moods rather than the highly activated, negative moods the researchers had expected. In other words, the watch was better at detecting that the body was “not relaxed” than at determining whether the person actually felt stressed. The authors concluded that “Stress Score” was a misleading name.Users don’t live in a laboratoryStress detection often looks impressive in the lab. Researchers can ask participants to rest and then complete a difficult mental arithmetic task or give a speech. Because the researchers created the stressful condition, they have a relatively clear reference point for interpreting the sensor data.Real life is much messier. You might be walking, digesting lunch, drinking coffee, and concentrating hard, sometimes all at once. Devices may also lose data because of movement, loose contact, cold skin, or poor circulation. People differ in age, medication use, health, baseline HRV, and how strongly their bodies react to the same event. Context matters, and a wearable device can’t capture most of it on its own.What do users actually say?User experiences are mixed. Some people find that tracking helps them recognize patterns or acknowledge strain they’ve been dismissing. Others find the readings confusing, unhelpful, or stressful.When the number contradicts how users feelIn online discussions and personal reviews, some Oura users describes a Daytime Stress graph that seems stuck on “Stressed,” even on days when they deliberately take it easy. When a reading repeatedly conflicts with their experience, it can become difficult to know what to trust.Clearer language could help. “Stress” is more marketable, but labels such as “bodily activation” or “signs of strain” would better communicate what the device measures. If an app uses the word “stress,” it should explain that the reading doesn’t necessarily mean someone feels overwhelmed.WHOOP app explaining what a stress score could mean (source)Some devices also ask users to record how they feel, bringing their own experience into the picture. For example, Fitbit can prompt users to log their mood after detecting a possible body response. This creates an opportunity to reflect, but the timing and frequency matter. Some users find repeated prompts annoying or say the notifications themselves make them feel more stressed.Fitbit prompting the wearer to check in after detecting bodily changes. (source)When there’s no clear next stepFor some users, tracking becomes useful when they can connect a reading to everyday experiences: a demanding day at work, drinking alcohol, or taking a quiet walk. But a score alone doesn’t offer much guidance. “Your score is 76” leaves plenty of questions: What caused it? Does it matter? What can I do about it?Simple tags and brief reflections can help people make sense of an ambiguous graph. An app could highlight possible patterns and suggest a manageable experiment. If readings often rise after poor sleep, for example, it could help the user explore that connection over time without treating it as a proven cause.When tracking becomes another source of pressureSome users describe feeling anxious after checking a stress graph. Tracking can become a loop: see a spike, worry about it, pay closer attention to the body, and check again. Others stop checking during the workday or stop wearing the device altogether.Design should leave room for people to step back, with adjustable reminders, optional summaries, and the ability to pause tracking. An interface also shouldn’t imply that lower activation is always better. Oura’s “Engaged” state is an example of this idea: it describes elevated physiological activation that may accompany focus and productivity rather than treating everything outside relaxation as negative. Color choices matter too. A simple green-means-good, red-means-bad scale can reinforce the idea that every increase is something to worry about.So, can stress really be quantified? Parts of it can, but making sense of those measurements still depends heavily on the user’s context and judgment. A device can detect physiological changes without fully understanding what’s happening in someone’s life, and results from a controlled lab don’t always translate neatly to everyday experience.
